name: Christian reconstructionism
summary: Christian reconstructionism is a Calvinist theonomic movement, founded by R. J. Rushdoony, Greg Bahnsen and Gary North, which holds that Old Testament civil law remains binding and that society should be rebuilt under Christ's lordship in every sphere. It expects gradual, postmillennial Christian dominion through regeneration, family, Christian schooling and church rather than revolution, favors a decentralized limited state and private property, and opposes statism and democracy as a source of authority.
scope: Christian Reconstruction (Christian reconstructionism): the fundamentalist Calvinist, theonomic movement developed chiefly by R. J. Rushdoony, Greg Bahnsen and Gary North, which holds that society should be rebuilt under Christ's lordship in every sphere, that the Old Testament civil law still binds, and that this comes gradually, from the bottom up. Sources: Rushdoony's own account of Chalcedon's vision, 9Marks's descriptive paper (which separates theonomic from non-theonomic reconstructionists and takes the theonomic strand as the movement's origin and leadership), Christianity Today's two 1990 reports, and reviews of McVicar's history. It excludes the non-theonomic reconstructionists, Christian-right politics that does not adopt theonomy, and unrelated early-20th-century works titled 'Christian reconstruction' (Douglass 1909 on Southern missions; Dickinson 1913 on the social gospel), which the downloaded books turned out to be.

missingStatements.text: Christians have a duty to take dominion over every area of life, including government, education and the economy.
missingStatements.rationale: Rushdoony: it is the duty of the state, the school, the arts and sciences, economics and every other sphere to be under Christ; Shupe: every institution of every nation is to be reclaimed for Christ.

missingStatements.text: Education is the responsibility of parents and the church, not the state.
missingStatements.rationale: Rushdoony wants health, education and welfare back in independent hands and promotes Christian and home schools; Clapp: parents will be responsible for the education of their children.
missingStatements.declined: Overlaps no-religion-state-schools and school-vouchers, which this audit leaves null; the position is not yet a distinct axis.

missingStatements.text: Old Testament civil laws and their penalties should still be applied by governments today.
missingStatements.rationale: Clapp: the Reconstructed society will form and administer law directly from the Old Testament, and Bahnsen holds the magistrate must enforce God's law; Shupe: Mosaic law is the blueprint.

notes: Strands differ: Bahnsen held biblical penalties need a Christian culture and cannot be imposed on an unwilling population, and Shupe and Clapp note that Reconstructionists disagree among themselves on many details. Later pass (2026-11-25): every answer was rebuilt from sources that name the movement, so answers that rested on inference, on Wikipedia or on Frame's review (which never names the movement) were nulled. Primary: Rushdoony's Chalcedon statement of vision and North and DeMar's 'Christian Reconstruction: What It Is, What It Isn't' (sample chapters: democracy, abortion, welfare, political action, the case laws); DeMar and Leithart, The Reduction of Christianity, read for pluralism and church-state (the 500+ page text was searched, not read through); Bahnsen's Always Ready was checked and has no theonomy content. Secondary and scholarly: Clapp's 'Democracy as Heresy' (Christianity Today 1987), Shupe (Christian Century 1989), Duncan (9Marks), Terrell and Moots on economics. Themes searched: law and penalties, democracy and republic, church and state, tax and welfare, economy and money, family and gender, schooling, race, foreign policy, pluralism, revolution. The sources read are silent on the movement's positions on foreign policy, immigration, race, unions, gun law, drugs, and most single-issue statements, so these stay null.
